title: ComplyAdvantage Alternatives: Replace It, or Add a Layer on Top
summary: ComplyAdvantage alternatives compared: seven replacements for screening and monitoring data, plus Sphinx for working the alerts your provider produces.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** ComplyAdvantage alternatives split into two groups: replacements for the screening and monitoring product (Napier AI, Flagright, LexisNexis, LSEG, Dow Jones, Moody's, OpenSanctions), and a layer such as Sphinx, which is not a screening data provider and works the alerts your current provider produces. The right group depends on whether your problem is detection or the queue behind it. The FCA's 2026 sanctions review found both: 75% of alerts on slightly varied names correctly identified the sanctioned party in its testing, and over a quarter of firms took three to five days to close name screening alerts.


Sphinx wrote this list. Sphinx is not a screening data provider, so it gets its own section rather than a number. The seven numbered replacements are products currently sold for screening or monitoring, described from their own published material and ordered by fit, not overall quality.


## What ComplyAdvantage Gets Right, and Why Teams Still Look Around


ComplyAdvantage's main product today is Mesh, a cloud platform launched in October 2025. Mesh runs Customer and Company Screening, Ongoing Monitoring, Transaction Monitoring and Payment Screening on shared customer data, with case management, risk scoring and a set of Agentic Workflows on top. Payment Screening moved onto Mesh in May 2026.


The strongest argument for staying is that ComplyAdvantage owns its risk data and the applications that use it. A team gets sanctions, PEP and adverse media intelligence from the same vendor that runs the matching, and ComplyAdvantage says critical sanctions lists refresh within minutes of publication. The company also publishes real pricing at the small end: a self-service Starter plan from $99 a month for up to 2,000 monitored entities, and a free ComplyLaunch program for early-stage start-ups. Its agents are a serious feature too. ComplyAdvantage states they resolve up to 85% of routine alerts, with agent and analyst actions in one audit trail.


Teams look elsewhere for reasons that have more to do with their own setup than with any flaw in the product. A bank's model risk or procurement group may want a second dataset with a different research method. A firm with data residency constraints may need on-premises deployment, and ComplyAdvantage describes Mesh as cloud-based. Some teams want the matching engine and the data on separate contracts so either can change on its own. Others run several detection systems and want one way of working alerts across all of them.


Before scoping a replacement, check where the ComplyAdvantage data already sits in your stack. Sumsub's AML screening and Dotfile's KYB workflow both announced Mesh integrations in 2026, so leaving one vendor contract may not take the data out of your program.

## First, Decide Whether Anything Needs Replacing


### Sphinx — Best for keeping your screening provider and working the alerts it produces


Sphinx is not a screening data provider. It maintains no sanctions database and does not generate the initial alert, so it cannot replace ComplyAdvantage's data or matching. It does the L1 work that follows.[Sphinx's AI compliance analysts](https://sphinxhq.com/products/ai-agents) log into the tools a team already uses, prepare the evidence, apply your SOPs, and produce a traceable recommendation; your team retains final approval. ComplyAdvantage is one of the platforms[Sphinx connects to natively](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/introducing-sphinx-browser-agents) .


Sphinx reports 87% fewer false positives on average, a 3.2-minute median case, and a 13-day median to go live, and Sia Partners independently validated its KYC, KYB and TM agents. Pricing is a platform fee plus usage tiers scoped to your volumes.


It suits teams whose detection works but whose queue does not, especially with alerts from several systems. The limit: Sphinx will not fix coverage gaps or missed matches, and a team on Mesh Enterprise with one detection stack should test ComplyAdvantage's own agents first.


## Seven Replacements, in Order of Fit


Sphinx is not on this numbered list, because it does not replace screening or data. The seven below are ordered by how much of Mesh each could take over on one contract: platforms that cover screening and monitoring, then screening products with their own data, then data sources.


### 1. Napier AI Continuum — Best for screening and monitoring together, with on-premises or private cloud options


Napier AI's Continuum platform covers Client Screening, Transaction Screening, Transaction Monitoring and Perpetual Client Risk Assessment, taken individually or together. Risk teams adjust rules and thresholds in a no-code sandbox, fuzzy name matching spans more than 20 languages, and agents support review with the decision left to a person. Deployment runs from fully managed SaaS to private cloud and on-premises, which is the clearest difference from Mesh.


Continuum suits banks and payment firms that want one platform for screening and monitoring but need control over where it runs. The limit comes from how the product is built: Napier describes its sanctions, PEP and watchlist data as coming from intelligence partners, so the feed needs its own evaluation. Its integration with LSEG's World-Check On Demand passed technology validation in October 2026, though neither company named a bank running it in production.


### 2. Flagright — Best for choosing your own watchlist data under one platform


Flagright combines Transaction Monitoring, Watchlist Screening, Case Management, Rule Simulation and Regulatory Filing, with AI agents that investigate hits and draft SAR narratives. Rules can be written in a no-code builder or in natural language, then simulated or run in shadow before going live. Its screening is data agnostic: teams can use native coverage powered by OpenSanctions and KYC6, connect a provider subscription they already hold, or add internal lists.


Flagright suits teams that want to change detection logic without engineering tickets and keep the choice of data open. The limit is the reverse of ComplyAdvantage's data ownership. Flagright does not present itself as the originator of risk data, so PEP and adverse media depth depends on the source you pick, and a premium feed may be a second contract.


### 3. LexisNexis Bridger Insight XG — Best for account and payment screening on one engine with the vendor's own data


Bridger Insight XG pairs a screening engine with LexisNexis's WorldCompliance data, which the company lists at more than 8 million risk profiles, 1,700 enforcement lists and 180 global sanctions lists. One engine handles account and payment screening, with batch and API access, configurable thresholds, audit trails and case management. Delivery options include single-tenant and multi-tenant cloud and on-premises installation. LexisNexis cites 60-80% false positive reduction with its advanced modules.


Bridger is closest to ComplyAdvantage's model on the screening side, since the same vendor supplies data and matching. It suits enterprises and payment businesses that want that pairing with hosting choice. The limit is scope: the Bridger pages describe account and payment screening, not behavioral transaction monitoring, so a team using Mesh for both would need a separate monitoring product.


### 4. LSEG World-Check — Best for World-Check data through screening software or an API


World-Check is a risk intelligence database covering sanctions, enforcement, PEPs and relatives and close associates, state-owned enterprises, and adverse media. World-Check One combines that data with screening software, ongoing rescreening, case management and an ISAE 3000-accredited audit trail. World-Check On Demand delivers the same intelligence through an API for embedded screening. In September 2026 LSEG launched Active Intelligence and World-Check Resolve, which suppressed an average of 74% of false positives in testing across 650,000 screening cases, by LSEG's account.


World-Check suits regulated firms that want the choice between a ready screening tool and API delivery from one data source. The limits are scope and timing. World-Check is a screening product rather than a behavioral monitoring one, and Resolve is new, so its testing figure has little production history behind it. Customer analysts still review and resolve the cases.


### 5. Dow Jones Risk and Compliance — Best for data feeds into your engine, or licensed news context


Dow Jones Risk and Compliance sells its datasets directly. The Watchlist feed covers sanctions and other official lists, PEPs, relatives and close associates, special interest persons, and entities sanctioned by control and ownership. Feeds arrive over SFTP in XML, CSV or Excel formats. For a hosted option, RiskCenter Advanced Screening and Monitoring adds matching, always-on monitoring and optional adverse media drawn from licensed news in Factiva.


Dow Jones suits teams that already run a matching engine and want to change only the data underneath it, and teams that care about the provenance of[adverse media](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/what-is-adverse-media-screening) . The limit follows from the feed model. A file-based feed supplies data, not detection, so your engine, thresholds and alert handling remain your responsibility. Transaction monitoring also sits outside what these products describe.


### 6. Moody's Grid — Best for adverse-media-heavy screening with optional review add-ons


Grid is Moody's risk database, which brings adverse media, sanctions, watchlists and PEPs together in structured profiles. Moody's lists more than 31 million risk profiles, 13,500 adverse media sources, 1,900 monitored lists and 7 million PEP records. Firms submit names through a web interface, batch file or API. Optional services, Grid AI Review and Analyst Review, filter results before they reach the client, and Client Alert Decisioning adds a review step for the firm's own team.


Grid suits firms with broad adverse media obligations that want filtering by risk type, stage and recency. The limit is scope, since Grid screens names rather than monitoring behavior. Treat the volume figures with care as well: every vendor counts profiles and sources in its own way, so the numbers on this page do not compare cleanly.


### 7. OpenSanctions — Best for in-house builds that need traceable, self-hosted data


OpenSanctions combines sanctions lists, PEPs and other public-interest data from more than 480 sources into one deduplicated dataset, updated four times a day. Every value links to a public source, the pipeline is open source, and the full dataset can be downloaded and inspected before signing a license. A matching API can run inside your own infrastructure, so customer PII never has to leave it. Commercial options include hosted screening billed by the query, a flat-rate internal license, and a reseller license.


OpenSanctions suits engineering-led teams and software providers who want full visibility into how the data is made. The limit is that it is a component. You supply the alert workflow, case management and monitoring, and the sources are public rather than proprietary research, so expect to assess adverse media separately.


## Five Questions That Settle the Decision


The question that matters most is where the failure actually sits. The[FCA's 2026 sanctions review](https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/good-and-poor-practice/sanctions-systems-and-controls-our-firms-our-findings) found that suspected breaches most often came from deficiencies in screening and alert management, which are two separate problems with two separate fixes.


1. Are you missing matches, or drowning in them? In the FCA's testing, 90% of alerts on exact names correctly identified the sanctioned party, against 75% on minor variations. Seed your own test file with[name variants](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/sanctions-screening-name-matching) , non-Latin scripts and long names, then run it through any candidate. If matches are the gap, look at replacing. If the[queue is the gap](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/why-are-screening-alerts-piling-up) , a new engine may only give you a differently shaped queue.
2. How fast are alerts closing today? The FCA found about 44% of firms resolved name screening alerts within one working day on average, and over a quarter took three to five days.
3. Do you need monitoring on the same contract? Mesh, Napier and Flagright cover it. The screening and data products here do not describe it, so moving to one of them likely splits your stack.
4. What does your payments flow need compared with onboarding? A[Federal Reserve working paper](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/files/2025092pap.pdf) found large language models cut sanctions false positives by 92% against the best fuzzy matching baseline, but ran over four orders of magnitude slower, and it proposed tiered designs for high-velocity payments. Ask each vendor which method runs at which point.
5. Can you explain the system to an examiner? The FCA noted firms that had to rely on a vendor to explain why certain names produced no alert. Ask for list update commitments, calibration documentation and access to match logic before you sign.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are the main alternatives to ComplyAdvantage?


For screening and monitoring on one platform, the closest options are Napier AI Continuum and Flagright. For screening with vendor-owned data, the options include LexisNexis Bridger Insight XG, LSEG World-Check, Dow Jones Risk and Compliance, and Moody's Grid. OpenSanctions fits in-house builds, and Sphinx fits teams that want to keep ComplyAdvantage and speed up alert work.


### Is Sphinx a replacement for ComplyAdvantage?


No. Sphinx is not a screening data provider and does not generate alerts, so a team still needs ComplyAdvantage or another screening source. Sphinx works the alerts that source produces: it prepares the evidence, applies your SOPs, and produces a traceable recommendation, and your team retains final approval.


### Does ComplyAdvantage have its own AI agents?


Yes. ComplyAdvantage offers Agentic Workflows on Mesh, with agents for Customer Screening and Ongoing Monitoring and for Transaction Monitoring. Its pricing page lists them under Enterprise rather than the Starter plan. A separate layer such as Sphinx makes more sense when a team runs alerts from several systems or wants the same SOP-driven review across them.


### How much does ComplyAdvantage cost?


ComplyAdvantage's pricing page lists a Starter plan from $99 a month for monitoring up to 2,000 entities, which covers screening, ongoing monitoring and adverse media. Enterprise pricing is on application and adds Transaction Monitoring, Payment Screening and Agentic Workflows. Early-stage start-ups can apply for the free ComplyLaunch program.


### How do you move off ComplyAdvantage safely?


Run the new system in parallel on the same population, compare alerts and misses, and recalibrate thresholds before cutting over. Export case history and audit trails before the contract ends, because[31 CFR 501.601](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-501/subpart-C/section-501.601) requires OFAC-related transaction records to be available for at least 10 years.
